--feed-full puts each entry's rendered body into <content type="html"> — product-spec §6.5.1 requires full-content inclusion to be an explicit option and this is it; without the flag every entry carries <summary> and no content. The content is the emitted <main>'s inner HTML, the same subtree §20.7 reads text from taken as markup, with EVERY href and src RESOLVED TO AN ABSOLUTE URL against the entry's own address (which §29.5 already put in <id>, so no new interpretation of a URL enters the product). The earlier claim that they could be left verbatim was false about §11.3: it prefixes root-relative href/src with the base's PATH only and sends the origin to og:/twitter: and canonical alone, while §11.1 leaves a page's own relative URL untouched — so an entry for blog/post.html carrying href="sibling.html" sent readers one directory up, and a subpath deploy carried /repo/pic.png rather than an absolute URL. The flag is a usage error without --base-url for §22.1's reason

Every URL the feed emits is checked as §21.6 checks a sitemap's — P13 located at the feed — and for a GENERATED feed this can only pass because of §29.4's third condition rather than an appeal to provenance: classifyCanonical answers `self` only for a canonical resolving to this page's own output path, so a canonical naming nothing emitted classifies unknown/elsewhere, that page is not an entry, and its unresolvable value never reaches the feed to be reported a SECOND time (it is already P13 at the page, §22.5, where the author can fix it). An authored feed.xml suppresses generation entirely and ships byte-for-byte (§21.5), which is not a corner case — the blog template's generator writes its own. ACTIVATION GOVERNS THE WHOLE SECTION INCLUDING THAT VERIFICATION (§21.1's rule): without --base-url a feed.xml is an ordinary mirror-copied asset and a broken root-relative reference inside an authored one publishes clean, because a site that shipped a hand-written feed built clean before §29 existed must keep building clean after it. A17 IS SUPPRESSED WITH GENERATION for a sharper reason: its sentence is `this page is not in feed.xml`, a claim about a file UNIFY wrote, and where the author supplies the feed unify cannot know whether the page is in it — raising it would be the invented claim §6.1 forbids, in the register that looks harmless

--search-index writes search-index.json at the output root; a FLAG rather than a consequence because nothing about a site declares that it wants one — there is no page-level statement meaning I am searchable, and inventing one would be the unify-only content schema product-spec §6.3.7 forbids templates from teaching. Top-level keys are schemaVersion and pages; a page's keys are url, title, description, headings, text in that order with no others; title/description are null when absent, headings [] and text ""; two-space-indented JSON with a trailing newline, pages in manifest order, byte-identical across builds; schemaVersion is 1 and changes only when a field's MEANING changes

Every value comes from a §20 record and nothing here reads a page: url is record.url and record.path when no --base-url was given (a root-relative reference is still an address a page on this site can link to, and refusing to emit without an address would make the flag useless for the local case it is most used in); membership is §21.2's predicate unchanged and shared — a record, indexable, not 404.html, self-canonical — because noindex means do not show this page in search results and a site search IS search results

text is FOLDED here, discharging the obligation §20.3 states and defers: every Unicode space separator (U+00A0, U+2000-U+200A, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000) becomes U+0020, runs collapse, the result is trimmed — so a reader typing an ordinary space finds a page that wrote U+00A0, which they could not against the unfolded field. NOTHING ELSE is folded: no case folding, no stemming, no stop-word removal, no truncation, no character count, those being a search engine's decisions and unify shipping no search runtime

audit --format json replaces §24.5's human report on stdout with one JSON document; --format human is the default naming the existing behaviour and any other value is a usage error naming both. pages holds the §20 records in manifest order — the same record every other feature reads, serialized, which is what product-spec §6.5.3 asks for by name rather than a summary of it — findings is §24.5's order so the two formats list the same things in the same sequence, and baseUrl is the assumed address or null. §14's problems and advisories still print to STDERR as prose and summary counts them, because putting them in the document would make this a second diagnostic channel and §14.1's contract is that there is one. Exit codes are §24.6's unchanged, a format flag that changed one being a second policy; each finding also carries `generated`, true when the page came from the --generate overlay (§33.4) — its own key rather than a decoration on `file`, which stays a plain path for consumers that resolve it

Each finding carries a stable fingerprint: a hex digest over id, source file, and the ONE datum distinguishing it from its siblings on the same page (the repeated id for id-duplicate, the field name for metadata-conflict, the unprefixed value for jsonld-url-unprefixed, the empty string where a finding occurs once per page). It EXCLUDES line numbers, evidence text and fix text: a fingerprint exists so CI can say this is the same finding I saw last week, so a fault surviving an unrelated edit above it must keep its identity through the line shift, and evidence/fix are prose (§14.1) whose rewording would otherwise retire every suppression. The digest joins the three fields with a separator that cannot occur in any of them, so no combination collides by concatenation

audit --external is the ONLY unify operation that touches the network, a flag precisely so that builds are offline and deterministic without qualification (§6.1). Scope is EXACTLY §12's reference set restricted to the values §12 skipped for being off-origin — one rule rather than a list, because §12 already answers what a reference is (href, src, srcset entries, poster, og:/twitter:, a meta-refresh target, JSON-LD URL properties, and url() in a stylesheet, a <style> block or a style attribute) and --external asks the same question of the same reader. An earlier draft enumerated four of those and called the list closed, which was a second interpretation of reference inside one product and the worse of the two, since an off-origin poster or url() is exactly what a link checker is for. Disallow: patterns are still not fetched and need no exception, §23.4 making them patterns rather than URLs so §12 never collected them. EVERY FAILURE IS A FINDING, INCLUDING ALL OF THEM: the unreachable-network usage error is deleted, because nothing available to a build distinguishes this-machine-has-no-network from the-one-host-this-site-links-to-is-down, and approximating it as every-probe-failed-to-connect made the commonest shape wrong — a site with ONE off-origin link, which is most sites, so the identical dead link reported as external-unreachable and exit 0 when some other URL happened to answer and as a usage error and exit 2 when it did not. ONLY http: and https: are fetched — fetch speaks those two and rejects anything else LOCALLY, which was being reported as the far end failing to answer, accusing a third party of being unreachable over a scheme unify never dialled — and EVIDENCE IS UNIFY'S OWN SENTENCE rather than the runtime's, since a thrown fetch error carries an implementation string while §24.5 makes evidence contract a reader and a diff depend on. HEAD falling back to GET on 405, each URL fetched ONCE per run, redirects capped at five, ten-second timeout, bounded concurrency, and the report ordered by §24.5's rule rather than by response order so two runs print the same bytes whatever the network did. external-unreachable is INCOMPLETE because the answer is about someone else's server at one moment rather than about this site's output — a link that 503s during a deploy is not wrong markup — which is also why this can never become a build check.

--format sarif is a MECHANICAL VIEW of §31.1's finding list and nothing more, which is the only condition product-spec §6.5.3 permits it under: id to ruleId, file to the artifact location, evidence to the message, fingerprint to partialFingerprints, broken to error and incomplete to warning, neither changing an exit code. The fix string is carried in PROPERTIES and not in SARIF's own fixes array, because SARIF 2.1.0 makes artifactChanges REQUIRED on every fix object while unify's fix is a sentence rather than a patch — a fixes array without it made every emitted document invalid against the schema, rejected by validators and by the code-scanning ingests the format exists for — and fix is not one of the five mappings either, both facts pointing the same way. Nothing is computed for SARIF that is not computed for --format json, and a future field needing a SARIF-only derivation is the signal this serializer has become an analysis path and must be removed rather than extended

Problem: a non-empty <include> whose target is not a .fragment.html (§32.2). Located at the include element and naming the target: a page or a layout is a complete document, so splicing content into one has no meaning, and the two things it might have meant — into its <main>, or into its body — are what layouts are for

Problem: a non-empty <include> whose target IS a .fragment.html but declares no <slot> (§32.2). Located at the include element and naming the fragment; the content would be dropped, which the content-loss law never permits

Problem: a <head>, <html>, or <body> element inside a fragment reached by a non-empty <include> (§32.3), located at that element — a fragment contributes no head and no root attributes, so the element would land in the body and do nothing, which is §10.5's shape one file type over

Problem: a fill inside a non-empty <include> naming a slot its target does not declare (§32.3). A PROBLEM rather than §7.3's advisory A02, and not as a severity preference: a page's unmatched fill stays in the page flow so nothing is lost, while a fragment has no flow — the include element is replaced entirely — so the content is dropped

Problem: a --generate script that threw (§33.2). Located at the generator's path, carrying the thrown message and, under DEBUG=1, the stack; the build stops BEFORE the scan, because a partial overlay is a site nobody described

An include's CONTENT decides which of two operations it is, and the split costs one sentence rather than a mode: an EMPTY <include> is verbatim, textual and pre-parse exactly as §5.1 has always said (whitespace between the tags is still emptiness), while a NON-EMPTY one is a composition — the target parsed, the include's children parsed, the two merged by §7's slot rules. An author who never writes content between the tags never meets the feature

A non-empty include is valid ONLY when its target is a *.fragment.html declaring at least one <slot>; both halves are required and each has its own problem (P25, P26), both located at the INCLUDE ELEMENT in the file that wrote it and naming the fragment too, because the fix is as likely to be in one file as the other

The merge is §7's unchanged: slot="name" replaces <slot name>, the consumed attribute is removed, an unfilled slot shows its own children, everything else replaces the bare <slot>, slots do not nest (P16), a <template>'s slots are never touched, and a repeated name draws A13 — the same rules from the same code reported the same way. Two subtractions follow from what a fragment is: NO head merge and NO root attributes (P27)

One fragment answers to both roles: an EMPTY include passes its <slot> elements through to the host, where a layout's composition consumes them (the established behaviour, unchanged), and a NON-EMPTY include consumes them itself. That is §32.1's split read from the fragment's side, and it lets one shared fragment be a layout's chrome in one file and a filled component in another without being written twice; what never happens is both at once, since a non-empty include consumes every slot in its target and an unfilled one shows its fallback rather than travelling outward

Fill scope is LEXICAL: content inside an <include> fills slots in that include's own target and nowhere else, so an <include> inside the fragment resolves against its own content and an unfilled slot there shows its own fallback. The alternative — a fill travelling down a chain until something matches — is action at a distance, where adding a slot to a deeply nested fragment silently changes what an unrelated page renders. Cycles remain P02, counted and printed the same way

Timing is unchanged and only the OPERATION differs: a non-empty include resolves in §2 step 2's same pass at the same moment, by parsing rather than splicing, so everything downstream sees one text and cannot tell which kind produced it; for a Markdown page §10.1's conversion-then-includes order is unchanged, which makes a non-empty include in Markdown an HTML block by the converter extension §10.1 already defines

What this is NOT: no props, no attributes passed to a fragment, no expressions, loops, conditionals or implicit data, no attribute merging anywhere, no style scoping, no reading the page from the fragment or the fragment from the page. Product-spec §6.4.1 conditions shipping on the rule still fitting the authoring-rules page: the MECHANICAL half is enforced by the line budget in tests/unit/docs-sync.test.js, and the EMPIRICAL half — the authoring trials docs/ratification-protocol.md specifies — is OWED rather than met and recorded as owed in docs/ratification.md, so the learnability claim stays an argument rather than a measurement until a round runs

--generate names a FILE IN THE SOURCE TREE, never a command: no shell, no argument list, no environment plumbing, and no way to express and-then-run-this-other-thing — a path is a thing the author wrote and can read, a shell string is a place arbitrary programs get spelled. The path resolves against the source root and must stay inside it (§4.3's containment rule, the same one includes and layouts obey), an escaping path being a usage error; it is saved in unify.yaml like any long option and applies to build, watch, dev and audit

The contract is entire: process.argv[2] is the absolute source root and argv[3] the absolute generated directory, with no module to import, no object passed in, no return value read and no callback; the working directory is the SOURCE ROOT. The runtime is unify's own, so a compiled binary runs a generator with no Node installed — the generator runs as a SUBPROCESS of that executable, its stdout passed through so a script that logs its progress still does, its exit status the whole of what unify reads back

Three consequences of the subprocess, normative rather than incidental: a generator calling process.exit() ends ITS OWN process and a non-zero status is P29 (unify does not sandbox arbitrary JavaScript and does not claim to, but the build must not carry on as though nothing happened); a generator that throws is P29 carrying the GENERATOR'S OWN MESSAGE, not the tail of the runtime's stack trace, with the whole of stderr passed through under DEBUG=1; and EVERY REBUILD RE-RUNS IT, structurally, because a new process has no module cache to consult — a cache returning the first build's copy would make every rebuild after the first silently skip the generator while reporting success, and a cache-busting query string does not achieve this because a runtime is entitled to ignore the query when caching a file URL, as Bun does

The generated directory is a fresh empty directory OUTSIDE the source tree, per build, removed after — which is what keeps src/ unmutated (so audit stays read-only and a failed build leaves nothing behind) and what makes the watch loop structurally impossible rather than filtered, since a generator writing into a watched directory would trigger the rebuild that runs the generator. Its files are scanned EXACTLY as source files are — pages, mirror copy, the underscore, .fragment.html — and --dry-run marks the row's origin, which it must, because a file in dist/ with no source behind it is otherwise unexplainable

A relative path present in BOTH trees is P12, naming the source file by its source path and the generated one as generated; neither wins, because last-write-wins is what §13 exists to forbid and either choice loses something silently — the source choice makes a generator's output vanish, the generated choice overwrites a file the author wrote. Replacing a page means deleting it; filling one in means writing it as a fragment and including it

The generator runs BEFORE §2 step 1, so it sees the source tree on disk and nothing else — no manifest, no composed pages, no output — which is the boundary that keeps this a seam rather than a plugin API: a generator cannot observe unify's intermediate state, so no change to that state can break one. A generator listing pages therefore reads the SOURCE files, exactly as it would if run by hand beforehand, which is what the blog template's own _scripts/gen.mjs already does

The boundary is stated because it cannot be enforced: unify runs the named file, does not sandbox it, and does not restrict what it reads or writes — §6.1 keeps UNIFY'S OWN build offline and deterministic and §6.7 says plainly that unify documents this boundary rather than policing it. Two guarantees remain and are what make the seam safe to USE rather than safe to TRUST: nothing the generator produces bypasses a check (a generated page is checked, its references are checked, its path collides like any other, and it publishes only inside §15's transaction), and a generator's failure is a build failure

The overlay and the source root are ONE RESOLUTION NAMESPACE, not merely one scan: every scanned file is named by its virtual path — its path relative to the root it was found under — and §4 through §13 resolve in that path space. §6.1 step 4's walk climbs virtual directories from the page's own up to the root, taking the first _layout.html any root holds at each level, so a generated docs/api.md discovers docs/_layout.html then _layout.html exactly as a hand-written page in the same position would; §5.1 steps 1-2 and §6.1 steps 2-3 resolve a /-rooted value from the namespace root and a relative one from the declaring file's VIRTUAL directory, so a hand-authored layout's <include src="/_includes/nav.html"> finds a fragment the generator wrote and a generated page's <include src="./sibling.html"> finds a file the author wrote. An implementation that joins the overlay to the scan alone fails twice for one reason: a generated page discovers no layout and publishes bare with no diagnostic and exit 0, and a generated fragment is invisible to <include>

Precedence in the namespace is THE SOURCE TREE: where one virtual path could be satisfied from both directories, the source tree's file is the one resolved — a generator able to shadow a file the author wrote would be the silent overwrite §13 exists to forbid. For a path that publishes the question never arises, because §33.4's P12 refuses the build first; it is observable only for paths that never publish, an underscore-excluded fragment or a _layout.html. Nearest still beats precedence inside the walk, because the namespace merges one DIRECTORY at a time rather than one TREE at a time: a docs/_layout.html the generator wrote is nearer to docs/api.md than the source root's and is the one that page gets

P29's detail quotes the generator's own words, so the runtime's INSPECTED ERROR OBJECT is dropped along with its code frames, carets, stack frames and version footer: a thrown Error's property block (`syscall: "open",`, `code: 'ENOENT'`) and the brace closing it are the runtime's presentation, not the author's message, and node's internal location header (`node:fs:560`) is dropped like its file one despite carrying no slash. Dropping keys on INDENTATION plus a JS identifier, which is what separates a machine-printed property from a generator's own line: an unindented line survives whatever it says, a generator listing `  first-post.md: no date` survives because a bare filename is not an identifier, and the three-line budget still exists for genuinely multi-line messages

generated and layout are the two PROVENANCE fields of §20.3, and §20.2's stated exception in full: layout is the source-root-relative path of the layout §6 resolved for the page and null when it composed with none (data-layout="none", layout: none, or no _layout.html above it), generated is which tree the page came from (§33.4). Neither is recoverable from the emitted bytes — composition consumes data-layout (§6.4) and the overlay is scanned exactly as the source tree is — so a consumer re-deriving either would be giving a second, freely divergent answer to a question the build already settled; both exist because a §24 fix line cannot be phrased truthfully without them, and the two values are the SAME ones §17 prints as "← page + layout" / "← page (no layout)" / "← generated", so the record and the report cannot drift. No further provenance is admitted: field sources, inlined includes, declared frontmatter and the layout text stay out
